extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical expositors, and students interested in proof exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating mathematical proofs and exposition emphasizing functions beyond mere logical correctness (explanation, communication, discovery, justification) from Rota's phenomenology essays. Targets authors and readers who want to make proofs truthful, informative, and productive for further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity of mathematical truth (depth/significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The predicate 'true' is a coarse abstraction; mathematical statements are judged along finer-grained levels (trivially true; true but uninteresting; true and useful; true and deep; true and beautiful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat every proved statement as of equal status. Explicitly indicate whether a result is merely a definitional unfolding (trivial), correct but without consequences, enables further work (useful), organizes a whole area (deep), or is true in a particularly revealing/beautiful way. A rubric that uses only 'correct/incorrect' misses these working-mathematician distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of a proof to establish the truth of a statement (logical correctness, validation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is necessary but not sufficient. Rota emphasizes that a proof that does only verification—even if logically correct—is incomplete. Evaluate whether the argument indeed establishes truth, but also whether it does more (see other criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation (why)
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of a proof to show why a statement is true—providing conceptual reasons, mechanisms, and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the proof illuminates the underlying reasons for the result rather than merely manipulating symbols. Good explanations connect the statement to intuition, reveal controlling ideas, and make the truth comprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication (conveys structure to others)
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of a proof in conveying its structure, dependencies, and main ideas to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge clarity of exposition: does the proof show which lemmas do the real work, present the structure in a way others can follow and reuse, and effectively organize material for different audiences? Communication includes clear organization, signposting, and transparency about difficult steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery / heuristic value
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's capacity to generate new conjectures, lemmas, or definitions and to guide further research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof suggests new directions, produces useful intermediate results, or contains heuristics that lead to additional theorems. Proofs that only close a case without yielding insight score lower on this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's role in showing that chosen concepts and definitions are appropriate—i.e., that they 'cut nature at its joints.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether definitions used are motivated and validated by how they function in proofs: do proofs reveal why those concepts are the right ones, or are definitions ad hoc? Good proofs help justify and illuminate the naturalness of definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful exposition / honest reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between giving a logically correct presentation and truthfulness in exposition: honest reporting of provenance, contributions of lemmas, locus of difficulty, and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for honesty about where ideas came from, which steps carry the burden of the argument, which parts are routine vs deep, and what the proof does not tell us. Avoid presenting an engineered or misleadingly streamlined narrative that hides the real genesis or difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking where the difficulty lies
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly indicate the parts of an argument that are genuinely hard or conceptually new versus routine reductions or calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good exposition flags the hard steps, explains why they are hard, and isolates the core obstacles. Do not bury difficulty inside lemmas without commentary; identify and explain the critical moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing expository synthesis and clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that synthesis, clarification, and reorganization of existing knowledge (expository work) are substantive mathematical contributions, not merely derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating work, give credit to efforts that reorganize or clarify theory, present cleaner proofs, or integrate disparate results. Expository contributions that illuminate and make material usable are first-class achievements in Rota's view.
